items.elements: One low, longer note dipping from about 4 to 3 kHz (0.25-0.5 s), then five short, evenly spaced chevron notes near 3.7 kHz (0.6-1.15 s), then a steep slide down from about 8 to 5 kHz that runs straight into a pulsed trill near 4.7 kHz (1.3-1.8 s). Faint background pulses near 5 kHz run through the whole cut.
items.phrase: Moan, tap tap tap tap tap, fall-and-shiver
items.grounds: The low drooping note became 'moan', the five short identical marks became five 'tap's, and the downward slide into a buzzy trill became 'fall-and-shiver'. I know the usual 'drink-your-tea' mnemonic for this species, but I left it out because this cut has five short middle notes, not one or two.
items.species: Eastern Towhee (the label given to me, not my own identification)

items.elements: A long, faint, steady whistle near 4.4 kHz that sinks slightly over 0-2.1 s, then three cleaner held whistles that step down: about 4.5 kHz (2.2-3.0 s), 4.0 kHz (3.1-3.7 s) and 3.2 kHz (3.75-4.85 s). Scattered chips from other birds sit in the background.
items.grounds: Four long, pure, held notes, the first the longest and the last three stepping down in pitch, so I chose four slow single-syllable words that fall when spoken. I know 'Old Sam Peabody' and 'Oh sweet Canada' for this species, but neither fits this falling, untrilled shape, so I used neither.
items.species: White-throated Sparrow (the label given to me)

items.elements: Two clean whistles: a higher one near 3.9 kHz that drops slightly to 3.6 kHz (0.23-0.63 s), then after a short gap a lower, level one near 3.1-3.2 kHz (0.73-1.2 s).
items.grounds: Two sustained notes, the second lower and a little longer, read like a two-word greeting whose second word drops. My knowledge of the 'fee-bee' song probably made me expect two notes and lean toward a greeting, though the picture shows the two notes plainly.
items.species: Black-capped Chickadee (the label given to me)

items.elements: Two faint rise-and-fall arcs (0.15-0.5 s and 0.6-1.0 s, about 2.5 to 6.5 to 3 kHz), probably a fainter call or another bird. Then the loud main song: a broad buzzy burst at 3-4 kHz rising a little (1.28-1.55 s), followed by a sharp, steep up-and-down note reaching very high (1.62-1.85 s).
items.grounds: The wide, noisy first block is buzz-like and the tall, steep, loud second stroke is a sharp exclaimed rise, so 'buzz' then a stressed 'WHEE'. Treating only the loud part as the song, and the arcs as something else, comes partly from what I already know of this species' short two-part song ('free-beer'); I did not use those words.
items.species: Alder Flycatcher (the label given to me)

items.elements: Two long upslurs rising from about 1.8 to 3.2 kHz (0.2-0.6 s and 0.9-1.45 s), then five short, quick downslurs falling from about 3.5 to 1.7 kHz, evenly spaced from 1.58 to 2.97 s.
items.phrase: Up? Up? Drop drop drop drop drop
items.grounds: Two long rising sweeps became two questioning 'Up?'s, and five short falling strokes became five clipped 'drop's. I know this species' 'what-cheer' and 'birdie birdie' mnemonics and avoided them, though knowing them may have shaped the rise-then-repeat framing.
items.species: Northern Cardinal (the label given to me)
